text: Wouter Addink. Thank you.
Hello, everybody.
My name is Wouter Addink.
I'm based at Naturalis Biodiversity Center in Leiden, the Netherlands,
which houses one of the largest collections in the world.
And I'm also representing DiSSCo here
as the technical director. And I'm going to tell you a little bit
about the plans for an annotation validation framework.
But before I do that, I would like to know who of you is
a curator of a natural history collection?
I see a few hands.
Most of you are not, but
assume for a minute that you are a curator. Yeah.
And that you are a curator of a typical collection, a
pretty large collection, a couple of million specimens,
and only about 10% of that is digitized.
And that digitized information is often of pretty low
quality. It's not georeferenced yet.
It is not having
identifiers for the collectors, for Binomia.
It contains
errors in the names, spelling errors, and things like that.
And you have a director of your museum, who is
a visionary director, and he is
informed about all the developments of AI, and he thinks, "Well, we can speed
up the digitization and improve the quality of your data
with use of AI." So that director
decides to give the technical team, the
developers of the museum,
to develop a annotation service with the help of
AI
that starts annotating the data, uses the
images from the collection to
transcribe the label information.
And, well, there is a pretty good software team at
the museum, so they succeed with that.
And the
machine annotation service they create
creates hundreds, maybe thousands, or maybe even millions of
annotations.
So pretty successful. So what is the result of that?
Well,
this is probably how the curator looks like now.
Like this.
A lot of stress because-
There are now thousands of annotations,
and what to do with that?
How to validate these annotations?
Do I trust these annotations? Do
I
maybe
accept that the annotation service automatically
puts the
data in
the collection management system?
If the
service does that and overrides the
records in the system, you lose the control over that, right?
So you lose the sovereignty.
But you also lose the provenance. So you lose the history of the changes in
the data. Of course, these things can
be fixed. We have seen that in the previous presentation.
These things can be fixed, but it's hard to do.
So it costs you a lot of effort at the museum to do that, and it also costs a
lot of effort to create this
AI-driven annotation system.
And this is exactly what the annotation validation
framework that we
want to implement in DISCO tries to solve.
With this, we want to enable
the running of machine annotation service, not at the museum, but
in the DISCO infrastructure.
And that means that
everybody can benefit from that
service. So if once you have created that service and you run it in the
infrastructure, you can run it not only on your collection, but you can
run it on all the collections that are in the DISCO infrastructure.
And
anybody can make an annotation in
the DISCO infrastructure, anybody with an ORCID and all the machine
annotation services can make annotations.
So you don't need to worry about that anymore in your
local collection management system.
And what we want to do, we don't want to have a system in
place where we say, "Well,
we accept this annotation. We don't accept that annotation."
That's not what we want to do. We want to have all the annotations
living happily together.
Right?
So we start, we create data layers, layers
of trust, where we want to place these annotations.
Because at the end, the annotations that we trust enough, we would like
to merge back into the digital specimen object,
so to have a single point of truth. So that is
the ultimate goal. That's the top layer here, the curated
consensus layer,
where we have the latest version of the
digital specimen object.
But we start with the institutional base layer.
So this, the data that we get from institutions, we are not going to
touch that. So,
the institution is in full control of that layer, and you can still use that layer.
But on top of that, we have that
community enrichment layer, where all the unvetted
annotations live. So everybody who makes an annotation,
all these annotations end up here, not validated.
And some of these annotations are just small error corrections, things like that.
And we can automatically
approve them, promote them to the curated consensus layer.
So we say, "Okay, we trust that these annotations are correct."
We promote them to the consensus layer.
But some of these annotations are things like
a suggestion for a new identification to change the scientific name,
or a suggestion to change the catalog number.
And these annotations have a high scientific impact, so these really
need a managed review. They need to be reviewed by experts.
And these experts can be humans, human experts, taxonomists,
but can also be machines. So once we have machines
that we can consider to be an expert, that we trust enough, we
can also automate part of that managed review process.
So the goal is to have a balanced
system where we want to automatically promote the
annotations as much as possible and only have to look at the
annotations that need further review.
So this is how the validation flow looks like.
You start
with the submission of a new annotation.
So that can be
an agent with an ORCID,
but that agent can also, that human can also
run a machine annotation service on
records.
And then, the annotation is created.
It gets a persistent
identifier and an ID of the agent, so we keep track of the
full provenance, the creation date, and things like that.
And then,
the step is followed by technical validation of that annotation.
So is the syntax correct? Does it follow the schema?
Does it follow the DISCO content policies?
For instance, does it not contain malicious content?
Does it not
provide an exact location of a
protected species?
Things like that.
This is a completely automated step, and once
it passes that technical validation, it enters the next
step, the automated routing of- ...
the annotation to one of these layers that I presented.
So it can be put in the open community
enrichment layer, the layer where all the unvetted
annotations live. It can be immediately promoted to the
consensus layer, or it can end up in the managed review layer, so
further review is needed.
And it ends with the promotion, the integration
into the digital object,
which creates a new version of the digital specimen.
And we store all the different versions over time,
so you can always go back to a previous version, and
this makes also the system very resilient, because if there
are some errors at some point in this automated
process, then we can always refer back.
This is the flow, how that works.
So
after the passing of the technical validation, we start
with the evaluation. What type of annotation is it?
Is it just a comment that is added, or is it
assessing data, so a quality flag?
So like this field needs to be checked, or that field is probably outdated.
Then we say, "Well, that's low impact." We put that in the community
enrichment layer,
because this is information that we cannot merge into the
digital object. It can also be
a proposal to delete the object,
because
it
may be a duplicate, it may be a digital specimen that already exists.
And this needs managed review by an administrator.
So this ends in the managed review layer.
The interesting part is where the annotation tries to add new data
or to edit existing data, or
to propose deleting of some of the data
within the digital specimen. Then it looks
like the impact. So it looks at the content of the annotation itself,
and it tries to assess the impact. And if it's
high impact, so it tries to correct an error in the type status,
or it
tries to create a new identification, then it is
considered high impact and it ends in the managed review.
If not, then it's maybe low impact.
So we use some algorithms to detect whether it's like an error
correction.
It's low impact, then we automatically promote that to the consensus view.
If not, if it's medium impact, then we say we need to
have a two-agent condition met. So two agents, for
instance, two machine annotation services, need to create the same
annotation, or an agent needs to
validate
the annotation of another agent.
Once that
condition is met, or the annotation is created by
an agent that has a good track record over time, that is a trusted agent,
then it is also promoted to that consensus layer.
These are two examples. So here you see a
low impact
example where you have an error correction.
So you want to correct this location
text,
and improve that and standardize that.
Other examples are measurements that are added.
We can just add them. So,
we have some automated checks for these kinds of annotations,
and we can automatically promote them to the consensus layer.
And this is an example of a high impact
annotation,
where a machine annotation service suggests a new scientific name.
I also mentioned the catalog number alteration, and this
needs a mandatory human peer review
by domain experts. And again, these experts can also be machines.
We are running a consultation on this because this is
just a plan at the moment.
We started that at the end of last month, so we aim to run this
consultation for
a month, until end of this month.
But I will give you a little bit more time if you want to look at this.
So, let's say to extend this public
consultation to the 16th of October, so with two
weeks.
I did not create a QR code for this because
the documents are very easy to find.
You can just go to the disco.eu website, and you
will find them on the homepage.
You can also look at the chat of this session, and you will find the link there
also. There are three documents in this plan,
and you should start with the general concept, because otherwise you will not
understand the other two documents.
We have also a document with the technical specifications, so all the nitty-gritty
details of the plan,
and a document with the conceptual governance model and the policy framework
behind that.
So this is what I had to tell. I invite you all to
look at this, because I think this is a very important development.
This is core to what we want to achieve with Disco.
So,
I ask for a call to action to all review these documents.
Send your comments via a form. I created a form for that.
On the 22nd of October, we have
an online meeting, and everybody is
welcome to join that meeting, where we are going to discuss the results, the
outcome of this consultation.
And after that discussion, we aim to finalize these documents
by the end of this year and then start implementation.
